issues: Section is approximately 420 words — exceeds the 380-word cap.

Third H3 block ('What Unbounce's messaging shift signals about message-match risk') contains two paragraphs that together exceed 60 words each: first analytical paragraph is ~75 words, second is ~55 words. First paragraph violates the 60-word per-paragraph rule.
The closing paragraph (founder takeaway / runnable test) is NOT under an H3 subheading — it floats outside any sub-block, making the section structure inconsistent.

The closing test instruction ('count how many measurable outcomes appear above the fold') is reasonably specific but anchors to a generic audit framing ('your own Unbounce-style homepage') rather than a precise, bounded action tied to this company's evidence.

The phrase 'build-test-optimise workflow' in H3-3 is an abstract noun stack (3 hyphenated concepts) without a plain-language unpacking in the same sentence — the inline definition 'a workflow where teams build pages, run tests, and improve results in one tool' appears after a dash, which partially rescues it, but the original phrase still leads.

Causal hedge is present ('may matter', 'may point to') but the claim 'that gap in relevance may matter' lacks an explicit condition — it is not stated under what condition (e.g., 'if paid search is a primary acquisition channel') the relevance gap becomes a conversion problem. A condition is implied but not stated explicitly.

The section does not reference the section-heading change from 'See How You Can Lower Cost-Per-Lead By Over 70% With Landing Pages' to platform-scope headings, which is strong evidence available in the evidence block and would strengthen the messaging-evolution argument.

No bold-quoted verbatim reference to any CTA or section heading changes within the messaging evolution analysis — the evidence includes section heading shifts that corroborate the messaging claim but are unused.

The opening of H3-3 does NOT lead with the finding in the first sentence — it leads with what was removed ('Removing... reduces...') before stating the implication, which partially satisfies FINDING-FIRST but buries the practical risk signal.
requiredFixes: Trim the section to under 380 words. The third H3 block and the floating closing paragraph are the primary sources of overage — tighten the closing paragraph to 2 sentences and remove the redundant re-explanation of the workflow definition.

Place the founder takeaway/runnable test inside a dedicated H3 subheading (e.g., '### Quick test: count the outcome signals above your fold'). The floating paragraph breaks the required H3 sub-block structure for analytical sections.

In H3-3, add an explicit condition to the relevance-gap claim. Example: 'if a significant share of Unbounce traffic arrives via high-intent paid search queries for terms like landing page builder, this gap in specificity may slow recognition' — make the 'if' clause explicit and front-loaded.

Cut the first analytical paragraph in H3-3 to under 60 words. It currently carries two distinct ideas (relevance gap for PPC visitors AND the new target being growth teams) — split them into two short paragraphs or cut the second idea, which is already covered in H3-1.

Add a single bold-quoted section heading from the evidence to H3-3 or H3-2 to anchor the messaging-evolution argument — for example, **'See How You Can Lower Cost-Per-Lead By Over 70% With Landing Pages'** dropped in favour of **'Convert more customers with one platform'** gives concrete proof of the ROI-to-capability shift.

Reframe the closing runnable test to be more precisely bounded: instead of 'count how many measurable outcomes appear above the fold', specify 'on your homepage, count the words that name a channel (paid, organic, social) or a metric (cost-per-lead, ROAS, conversion rate) in the first 50 words of body copy — if the count is zero, you have made the same trade Unbounce made.'
riskFlags: 'This suggests the page is no longer written for the PPC manager' — causal inference without explicit condition stated; partially hedged but condition is implicit, not explicit.

'that gap in relevance may matter' — consequence claim without a stated condition (e.g., only if paid search is the primary acquisition channel); the condition is implied but must be made explicit per rubric.

'That shift may point to a larger addressable market' — this is speculative and not directly traceable to the evidence; the evidence notes a buyer-shift hypothesis but does not confirm TAM expansion. Flag as unsupported.

The word 'signals' in H3-3 heading implies a definitive read of intent; evidence note says 'The change in framing may reflect a positioning adjustment or an SEO update' — the heading should hedge accordingly.
seoNotes: The ## section heading contains both 'H1' (a searchable structural term) and 'ROI' and 'buyer' — it passes the searchable heading check, though 'messaging' or 'Unbounce' would strengthen it further.
The section does not use the primary keyword 'Unbounce homepage teardown' in any H3 heading — adding it to at least one H3 would improve keyword density for the target query.

The meta description shift from 'Ditch your other landing page software' to 'AI insights' is a strong SEO signal about competitive positioning that the section covers well — this is the most linkable insight in the piece and is correctly foregrounded.

The page title evolution from 'Landing Page Software' to 'CRO platform' is noted in H3-2 and is a strong secondary keyword signal — consider adding a one-sentence note that this title shift also affects how Unbounce appears in SERPs for CRO-related queries, not just landing page queries.

Pull in one bold-quoted section heading from the evidence (the old CPL claim vs the new platform claim) to anchor the messaging-shift argument with a third proof point beyond H1 and meta.
